Activation steering works by adding a direction vector (typically extracted via contrastive pairs or PCA over activations) to the residual stream at inference time to push model behavior toward some concept. The central question here is: when you compose multiple such vectors simultaneously — say, steering for "French" and "angry" at once — do their effects combine linearly and independently, or do they interfere destructively, reinforce unexpectedly, or collapse into something neither vector intended? The worry sharpens in superposition-heavy layers, where the residual stream is simultaneously encoding far more features than it has dimensions (Elman-style polysemantic compression), meaning your steering vector is virtually guaranteed to have non-zero projections onto dozens of unintended feature directions — you're never just touching the concept you think you're touching. What a beginner misses is that interference isn't symmetric: some concept pairs share geometric neighborhood in activation space (their directions are nearly parallel or lie in the same low-dimensional subspace) while others are nearly orthogonal, and the failure modes are totally different — parallel vectors amplify each other's crosstalk, while orthogonal ones may compete for representational bandwidth during residual accumulation across layers. An expert also worries about layer-specificity: a vector extracted from layer 15 implicitly encodes not just the concept but that layer's particular superposition basis, so composing two vectors extracted from different layers and applying them together at a single layer is doing something theoretically incoherent that practitioners rarely audit.

The geometric property you want is near-orthogonality between the two steering vectors — specifically, a cosine similarity close to zero — because orthogonal directions in the residual stream make independent additive contributions under linear superposition, meaning each vector's projection onto the other's direction is negligible and cross-contamination is minimized. Anthropic's dictionary learning work on Claude (the "Towards Monosemanticity" line) operationalizes this intuition: sparse autoencoder features that are nearly orthogonal tend to activate independently, which is the learned-feature analogue of what you want steering vectors to do at inference time. But orthogonality is necessary, not sufficient, for at least two concrete reasons. First, even perfectly orthogonal vectors can both have large projections onto a third shared "hub" feature direction — a polysemantic neuron that participates in both concepts — and steering along both simultaneously over-activates that hub in a way neither vector alone would predict; Elhage et al.'s 2022 superposition paper shows that features in superposition are arranged in antipodal pairs and pentagons specifically to minimize such interference, so real models don't give you clean orthogonality for free. MLP sublayers pose the greater threat to steering fidelity, and the mechanism is the nonlinear activation function — typically GeLU in modern transformers — which breaks the linear superposition that makes steering vectors theoretically tractable in the first place. Concretely, an MLP computes something like FFN(x + v) where v is your injected steering vector; if the pre-activation values W(x) are near the saturation or transition region of GeLU, then adding v shifts neurons across the nonlinearity's knee, producing output changes that are not proportional to v and not predictable from the network's behavior on x alone — this is the "nonlinear folding" problem. Anthropic's work on MLP neurons as "memory" (the Geva et al. 2021 "Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories" framing, extended in the superposition papers) implies that individual MLP neurons function as soft feature detectors with nonlinear thresholds, so your steering vector activates a different set of neurons than the natural residual stream would, introducing spurious feature activations that compound across layers. Attention sublayers are comparatively more forgiving because the value-weighted aggregation is linear in the values given fixed attention weights — your injected direction passes through attention mostly intact, diluted by the softmax-weighted average over other token positions but not fundamentally distorted in direction. The key asymmetry is that attention's damage is primarily attenuation (your vector gets mixed with other positions' representations), while MLP's damage is rotation and hallucination of new components — you lose the direction and gain contamination. Numerically, Hernandez et al. (2023) on linearity of factual associations found that fact-recall vectors survive attention relatively cleanly but degrade measurably after deep MLP stacks, which is consistent with this picture.

This is mechanistically cleaner because you're respecting the model's natural computational schedule: concept A's direction is established at layer 12, you inject there, it propagates forward and gets partially encoded into the residual stream, then at layer 18 you inject concept B's direction into a stream that already carries A's influence — the composition happens via the model's own forward pass rather than by vector addition in a single layer's input. The most predictive pre-forward-pass property is the relationship between each steering vector and the model's embedding weight matrix — specifically, how well each vector projects onto the subspace spanned by the token embedding matrix's principal components, which approximates the "output-legible" subspace that the residual stream must occupy for the unembedding layer to decode coherent tokens. Concept pairs where both vectors have high projection onto this output-legible subspace but point toward overlapping regions of it are high-risk for silent failure: the two vectors are both "loud" to the unembedding layer but compete to express different things through the same output channels, and the resolution is typically a fluent compromise that satisfies neither — analogous to two signals interfering constructively in amplitude but destructively in meaning. A second computable predictor is the condition number of the matrix formed by stacking your two steering vectors as rows: a high condition number (one vector much larger in norm or the two nearly parallel) predicts that the composed perturbation is numerically dominated by one vector, suppressing the other silently rather than producing the noisy activation collapse that triggers inference-time alarms. Conversely, pairs at high risk for noisy failure have vectors that both project substantially onto the null space of the output embedding — directions the model has never learned to decode — producing norm inflation and entropy explosion that are detectable but not semantically interpretable. Park et al.'s 2023 work on the geometry of concept representations found that "linearly represented" concepts cluster near the embedding subspace with cosine similarities to the top-50 PCA components of the embedding matrix often exceeding 0.6, while poorly-represented concepts scatter outside it — giving you a per-vector score whose product across two vectors roughly indexes silent-failure risk. The practical takeaway is that before composing any pair, you should compute each vector's projection mass onto the unembedding's top principal components and their mutual cosine similarity within that projected subspace: high projection mass on both plus high intra-subspace similarity is the silent failure signature, while low projection mass on either is the noisy failure signature.
